Title: The cynical truth about the name change

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
pe...@homer.ucsf.edu.ucsf.edu (Eric Pettersen) writes:

> WotC's had two choices: drop Jyhad completely, or try to obfuscate
>the second edition past retailers by changing the game's name and removing
>any links to the previous name, including card backs. Changing the card
>backs was a painful decision, but it was far too dangerous to retain the
>old backs: the game would be too easily recognizable as Jyhad. WotC has
>tried to justify the name change on moral grounds or as a means to penetrate
>new markets, but the real reason for the change is that they have made
>the name Jyhad economic poison.

That's totally absurd. When you consider that almost all the cards are going
to be identical (with the same artwork, purpose, etc., if not always the
exact same card text) and the card backs are going to have the same green
marble background with one word changed, no sane person would think that
changing that one word would disassociate V:tES from Jyhad. Besides, one of
the reason retailers are having so much trouble moving those cards these days
is that anyone who's not thoroughly incensed by the card back change such
that they would still consider buying V:tES is going to wait for the V:tES
cards to come out for totally obvious reasons. In short, the sales problems
(to the extent that they didn't already exist) are due to the card back
change, not the other way around.

Fred

Messages.Author: Eric Pettersen
Messages.Body:
WotC tells us that the name "Jyhad" offends their Mid-East
distributor. What they don't tell you is that Jyhad offends _all_ their
distributors and all their retailers. They're not morally offended;
they're financially offended. WotC soaked them with Jyhad.
It's all because of WotC's short-sighted, egotistical and greedy
decision to print 180 million Jyhad cards in the "limited" (what irony)
edition. They sold all 180 million. Distibutors and retailers seeing
Jyhad as the Next Big Thing from WotC, the company with the Midas touch,
the company that could do no wrong, snapped up the cards. Unfortunately
Jyhad was not the Next Big Thing. It was the next reasonably successful
but-no-MtG thing. Which means that distributors and retailers couldn't
sell anywhere near as many cards as they had on hand.
Here in San Francisco, for example, no CCG outlet is out of stock
for Jyhad despite the "limited" edition and the second printing being
overdue. One store has had Jyhad "on sale" for months now; starters $5
and boosters $1.50. I went in recently and, not spotting the Jyhad
immediately, asked them if they still had Jyhad starters. "Yes." the
sales clerk groaned, "hundreds." It's not hard to get a box of boosters
for $50 at any convention. At Manafest recently, one dealer was selling
boxes of boosters for $25 each! The dealer did manage to move all his
boxes at that price (a loss), most to another dealer. A friend of mine
asked the dealer why he was selling so low and the dealer replied that he
had had the boxes for months now and couldn't afford to have that much
money tied up in inventory so he had to sell them for what he could get.
Getting the picture? The name Jyhad is completely dead as a CCG
that you can market to retailers. Picture a retailer reading promotional
material for a forthcoming "umlimited edition" of Jyhad! He'd look at
his slow-moving inventory of dozen of boxes of "limited edition" Jyhad
and be rolling around on the floor laughing. "The Dark Sovereigns expansion
to Jyhad"; another gale of uncontrollable laughter.

WotC's had two choices: drop Jyhad completely, or try to obfuscate
the second edition past retailers by changing the game's name and removing
any links to the previous name, including card backs. Changing the card
backs was a painful decision, but it was far too dangerous to retain the
old backs: the game would be too easily recognizable as Jyhad. WotC has
tried to justify the name change on moral grounds or as a means to penetrate
new markets, but the real reason for the change is that they have made
the name Jyhad economic poison.

---
Eric Pettersen
pe...@cgl.ucsf.edu (NeXTmail capable)

Messages.Author: Joseph Cochran
Messages.Body:
In article <3v9c09$s...@murrow.corp.sgi.com>,
Chad McDaniel <ch...@engr.sgi.com> wrote:
>I disagree with your final point. I do think that one >good< reason for
>changing the name (regardless of the cardbacks) is that it more clearly
>communicates what the game is about. I have encountered many people who are
>muddled by the name Jyhad, but become interested when I mention that it is
>about vampires.

It's all marketing. White Wolf put out a game called "Rage",
and nobody I know didn't get the impression that it was about
werewolves. Why? WW are masters of flashy marketing (noseroids aside).
Jyhad would've been a fine seller if they had marketed it as a game about
vampires. Instead, it's marketed (look at the box) as a "Deckmaster"
game by Richard Garfield (by that I mean that the front of the box, the
prime eye-catching space, never once implies vampires, and if you turn
it over, more often than not the gold stripe of the cellophane around
the box is positioned right over top the "Vampire: the Masquerade"
name. Rage, on the other hand, has a werewolf on the front, and
mentions the Werewolf game right on the front).
I don't buy that Jyhad's lack of sales was because of the name.
It was because of poor marketing to the intended audience (and because
of complexity of rules, but that's not a bad thing).

We printed Jyhad based on pre-orders. We were actually somewhat skeptical that
that much limited edition of any game could sell, but what do you think the
reaction would have been if we had said "Sorry, we refuse to sell you all
those cards?" People might have understand that *now*, but would they have
then? Of course not; everyone was assuming it would be the next Magic.

Yes, Jyhad was overprinted for a limited edition game. But we gave the
distributors and retailers what they asked for.

>They sold all 180 million.

Actually, that's not true.

>Distibutors and retailers seeing
>Jyhad as the Next Big Thing from WotC, the company with the Midas touch,

>Jyhad was not the Next Big Thing. It was the next reasonably successful
>but-no-MtG thing. Which means that distributors and retailers couldn't

Well, then they guess wrong on how much Jyhad they could sell. They
overordered without having seen the game. Speculators probably fueled
a lot of that market. But we didn't force the cards on anyone; people
ordered them.

> Getting the picture? The name Jyhad is completely dead as a CCG

>his slow-moving inventory of dozen of boxes of "limited edition" Jyhad
>and be rolling around on the floor laughing. "The Dark Sovereigns expansion

Well, that retailer either a) got in after Jyhad was released, so doesn't
understand the history, or b) was part of the ordering binge, so should
know exactly what went on, and accept that he/she was most likely
part of the problem.

No, we aren't sticking the retailers, or the distributors, with all of the
blame (such as there is) for the overprinting of Jyhad. But the blame is
quite clearly shared by all.

> WotC's had two choices: drop Jyhad completely, or try to obfuscate
>the second edition past retailers by changing the game's name and removing
>any links to the previous name, including card backs. Changing the card

This is a nice conspiracy theory, but it has little to nothing to do with
reasons for changing the name and card backs.

^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

Magic has been out for *two years*. Think about that. Overhead for producing
the game has gone up a lot in that time. Exchange rates change, the price of
paper of all kinds is going up all over the world, etc. It was simply not
economically feasible to continue selling the game at the old prices. One
cannot stay in business by taking a loss every time one sells product. Well
it would be swell and great if the price of Magic (and our other products)
never changed, that's not how reality works.

You know, you could be right. But I wouldn't dismiss the idea so
lightly if I were you. That one word on the card backs is critically
important in convincing retailers that VtES is, in fact, for all intents
and purposes a new game. The name is different, the rules are different,
the card fronts are _noticeably_ different (the text of many cards is
changed and more importantly the black borders are replaced by different
colors for different card types), and finally the card backs _are_ different.
If the card backs didn't change, then the assertion that VtES is a different
game would be substantially weakened.
The real test as to whether the name change was motivated by
deceiving retailers will occur when VtES actually comes out. If it is
virtually impossible to tell that V:tES was Jyhad from the exterior packaging
and marketing displays for VtES, then I think it would be clear what
motivated the name change.
By the way, I think that your assertion that Jyhad sales problems
are due to the card back change (i.e. there is some large market of people
that don't yet own many Jyhad cards and are just waiting for VtES) is
absurd. :-)

Robert Matthew Edens <red...@gladstone.uoregon.edu> wrote:

>printing? Here's an even more novel idea( don't give me the C*R*A*P about
>how you can't find a printing house in the states either, I know people
>who run printing houses and they could do the job _easily_):

You'd think it would be easy, but it isn't. Printing houses simply aren't
set up to handle the kind of requirements that deckmaster games have. And
the cards *do* have to be identical to what Carte Mundi produces. If the
card dimensions are off by even 1/100 of an inch, you can pick the larger
card out of a deck of smaller ones almost infallibly. We also need to make
sure that the paper and finish are the same, that they can collate the
cards reasonably, etc. It's not really a question, at this point, of finding
print houses *willing* to do the job. It's a question of finding ones that
are *able* to, or willing expand their facilities appropriately, and that
can charge competitive rates.

Messages.Author: Thomas R Wylie
Messages.Body:
Karl J. Hiller <br...@iglou.iglou.com> wrote:
>Why would this be a problem? Are you suggesting that being able to tell
>the difference between two sets of cards might affect the game in some
>unwanted way? Be careful, now...

As I have stated several times during the card back debate, being able
to tell something about the top card on the library is a lot less interesting
than being able to tell something about any given card in the library.
Mixing alpha cards in with non-alpha cards, in Magic, gives you much more
information about what's coming up than only being able to know something
about the top card.
